title: The Pleasure of Fear in 17th-Century Musical Theater
content: In 1974, Richard Alewyn argued that the pleasure of fear, as represented by the 'uncanny', was an aesthetic post-Enlightenment phenomenon. In order to evaluate this thesis, it is necessary to investigate artefacts from the pre-Enlightenment era. This article therefore focuses on 17th-century music theatre, searching for clues to the pleasure of fear and the uncanny in such works. After investigating examples from La Pellegrina (Intermedio), Cavalieri's Rappresentazione di Anima, et di Corpo, Monteverdi's Ballo delle Ingrate, Lully's Béllérophon and Alceste, Purcell's Dido and Aeneas, and Charpentier's Médée, as well as contemporaneous descriptions of these performances, the article concludes that pre-Enlightenment art did imply the pleasure of fear, and possibly the uncanny. However, three observations can be made in contrast to post-Enlightenment art: 1) The horrible agents in 17th-century music theatre do not usually occur of their own accord, but are intentionally evoked by human agents; 2) The horrible is not usually the subject itself, but comes into play as part of a love drama or similar; 3) 17th-century music theatre does not thematise the disturbance of a natural order; rather, the monsters simply belong to the fictional reality.
